_readme: Hand-verified figures that have no machine-readable feed. Every value must be read from the cited source. When a source updates: change the values, set verified_on to today, set recheck_by to the next expected release. The daily pipeline flags any metric whose recheck_by date has passed and checks every URL still resolves.

metrics.title: Gross government debt
metrics.question: Is the Commonwealth's debt going up or down?

headline.caption: gross debt: above $1 trillion for the first time

benchmark.label: When the government took office (30 June 2022)

metrics.status_rule: Off track if gross debt (in dollars) is forecast to be higher than at 30 June 2022.
context: At 30 June 2006 gross debt was $54.1 billion (5.4% of GDP). It reached $257.4 billion in 2012–13, $542.0 billion in 2018–19 and $895.3 billion (38.3% of GDP) at 30 June 2022, when this government took office.
It was $928.6 billion at 30 June 2025, the latest audited actual. The Budget forecasts $1,051 billion by June 2027 and $1,249 billion by June 2030: above $1 trillion for the first time.
As a share of the economy, gross debt peaked at 39.1% of GDP in 2020–21 and fell to 33.4% in 2024–25. The Budget forecasts it rising again to peak at 35.8% in 2028–29.
Net debt is forecast to rise from $532.3 billion (2024–25) to $767.8 billion by 2029–30.

chart.note: Face value of Australian Government Securities on issue at 30 June, 2005–06 to 2029–30. Lighter bars are 2026–27 Budget estimates (rounded to the nearest $1 billion). Hover a bar, or open the data table, for debt as a share of GDP.

sources.title: Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 11: Historical Australian Government Data
sources.table: Table 11.5 (pp. 434–435): face value of AGS on issue, 'Total AGS on issue', $m and % of GDP, 2005–06 to 2029–30

sources.title: Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 3: Fiscal Strategy and Outlook
sources.table: Table 3.1 note (c), p. 85: 'Gross debt measures the face value of Australian Government Securities (AGS) on issue'

sources.title: Final Budget Outcome 2024–25
sources.table: Table B.5 (pp. 105–106): Total AGS on issue, independent cross-check of 2005–06 to 2024–25

metrics.method: Face value of Australian Government Securities (AGS) on issue at 30 June ('Total AGS on issue' column, Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27 Table 11.5), which the Budget defines as gross debt. 2005–06 to 2024–25 are actuals, identical in the 2024–25 Final Budget Outcome. 2025–26 onward are Budget estimates rounded to the nearest $1 billion. Share of GDP uses the GDP figures in the 2026–27 Budget. Actual years are cross-checked automatically every day against the AOFM register of securities on issue.

explainer.what: Gross debt is the face value of all bonds and Treasury notes the Commonwealth has issued and not yet repaid: the amount it must pay back to investors when they mature. It is a snapshot at 30 June each year. Net debt, a separate measure, subtracts certain financial assets the government holds.
explainer.why: Debt has to be serviced. Every dollar of interest is a dollar not spent on services or returned as tax cuts, and higher debt leaves less room to respond to the next crisis. The long view shows how debt has built up over two decades and where it is forecast to go.

metrics.title: Budget deficits
metrics.question: Is the government living within its means?
metrics.status_rule: Off track if the government's own Budget forecasts a deficit for the current financial year.
context: The budget recorded surpluses in 2022–23 (+$22.1 billion) and 2023–24 (+$15.8 billion), then returned to deficit in 2024–25 (−$10.0 billion).
The 2026–27 Budget forecasts a deficit in every year of the forward estimates: −$28.3b, −$31.5b, −$31.0b, −$34.4b and −$25.3b from 2025–26 to 2029–30.
Tax receipts are forecast at 23.8% of GDP in 2026–27, up from 23.0% in 2021–22. The tax take is higher as a share of the economy, but payments have risen faster (see Government spending).

chart.note: Red = deficit. Lighter bars are Budget forecasts. 2021–22 was the final budget year of the previous government.

sources.title: Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 11 (Table 11.1: underlying cash balance; Table 11.3: tax receipts)

metrics.method: Underlying cash balance (general government sector) as published in Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Table 11.1. Years to 2024–25 are actuals; later years are estimates.

explainer.what: The underlying cash balance is the Commonwealth's headline budget result: cash receipts minus cash payments, excluding the Future Fund's investment earnings. A negative number is a deficit.
explainer.why: Deficits are funded by borrowing, which adds to debt and interest costs. Deficit spending also adds to demand at a time when the Reserve Bank is trying to bring inflation down.

metrics.title: Interest on government debt
metrics.question: How much are taxpayers paying just to service the debt?
metrics.status_rule: Off track if annual interest payments are higher than in 2021–22.
context: Interest payments are forecast to rise from $17.4 billion in 2021–22 to $29.6 billion in 2026–27 and $42.3 billion by 2029–30.
The Budget itself says interest payments are expected to peak at 1.6% of GDP in 2032–33.

In 2026–27 the government expects to spend more on public debt interest ($31.9 billion, accrual basis) than on transport and communication ($15.3 billion) and public order and safety ($9.7 billion) combined.

chart.note: Cash interest payments, general government sector. Lighter bars are Budget forecasts.

sources.title: Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 11 (Table 11.4: interest payments)
Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27 (Table 6.3: expenses by function; Table 6.17: other purposes)
Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 3: Fiscal Strategy and Outlook

metrics.method: Interest payments (cash) from Budget Paper No. 1 Table 11.4. The comparison with other spending uses accrual expenses by function (Tables 6.3 and 6.17), which is why public debt interest expense ($31.9b) differs from cash interest payments ($29.6b).

explainer.what: The interest the Commonwealth pays each year to the investors who hold its bonds. It rises when debt grows and when interest rates on new borrowing are higher.
explainer.why: Interest buys nothing: no hospitals, no defence, no tax relief. It is a direct cost of past and present deficits, and future taxpayers carry it.

metrics.title: Government spending
metrics.question: How big is Commonwealth spending compared with the economy?

headline.caption: of GDP spent by the Commonwealth

metrics.status_rule: Off track if Commonwealth payments as a share of GDP are above the pre-COVID 2018–19 level.
context: Payments are forecast at $829.6 billion in 2026–27, up from $616.3 billion in 2021–22.
Spending was 24.3% of GDP in 2022–23. It has risen every year since and is forecast at 26.8% in both 2026–27 and 2027–28.
The 2021–22 figure (26.4%) still included pandemic support. Before COVID, in 2018–19, spending was 24.5% of GDP.

chart.note: 2025–26 onward are Budget estimates. Financial years ending 30 June.

sources.title: Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 11 (Tables 11.1 and 11.3)

metrics.method: General government sector cash payments and tax receipts as a percentage of GDP, Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 11.

explainer.what: Total Commonwealth cash payments (welfare, health, defence, grants to the states, interest and so on) as a share of Australia's GDP. Tax receipts are shown for comparison.
explainer.why: It shows the size of the federal government relative to the economy. When spending grows faster than the economy, it must be paid for with higher taxes, more debt, or both.

metrics.title: Size of the public service
metrics.question: How fast has the Canberra bureaucracy grown?

headline.caption: growth in Australian Public Service (APS) headcount

metrics.status_rule: Off track if APS headcount has grown more than twice as fast as Australia's population over the same period.
context: The APS grew from 159,179 employees at 30 June 2022 to 198,529 at 30 June 2025: 39,350 more public servants.
The Budget estimates the APS Average Staffing Level at 217,256 in 2026–27.
The government says about 13,200 of the new roles replaced external contractors and consultants, around one-third of the increase in staffing since 2022.

chart.note: Ongoing plus non-ongoing employees at 30 June each year.

sources.title: State of the Service Report 2024–25: APS workforce size and location (Table 10)
APS Employment Data, 30 June 2022
Budget Paper No. 4 2026–27: Staffing of agencies
Budget Paper No. 4 2026–27: Preface (external labour conversions)

metrics.method: APS headcount (ongoing + non-ongoing) from APSC data at 30 June. The population benchmark is the change in ABS estimated resident population between the June quarters of the same years, computed automatically from the ABS Data API.

explainer.what: The Australian Public Service is the federal bureaucracy: departments and agencies such as Services Australia, the ATO and Home Affairs. It does not include the military, state public servants, or staff of government businesses.
explainer.why: Every public servant is paid by taxpayers. Growth can mean better services, or more administration, regulation and cost. We compare it with population growth to see whether the bureaucracy is growing faster than the country it serves.

metrics.title: NDIS cost growth
metrics.question: Is the government meeting its own target to rein in NDIS cost growth?
metrics.status_rule: Off track if annual NDIS cost growth is above the 8% growth target agreed by National Cabinet.
context: NDIS expenses rose from $28.6 billion in 2021–22 to $46.5 billion in 2024–25, and were $50.2 billion in the 12 months to March 2026.
The government's own impact analysis says the 8% target 'would not be met by July 2026'. A new target of 5–6% growth was set in January 2026.
The 2026–27 Budget puts NDIS expenses at $56.1 billion, including state contributions. The scheme supports 774,456 participants (March 2026).

sources.title: Estimates brief: NDIS expenses (FOI 25-26/146)
NDIS Reforms Impact Analysis (1 July 2026 update)
Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27 (Table 6.9.2)

metrics.method: Scheme expenses by financial year from the Department of Finance estimates brief. Latest 12-month growth and participant numbers from the NDIS Reforms Impact Analysis.

explainer.what: The National Disability Insurance Scheme funds support for Australians with permanent and significant disability. It is jointly funded by the Commonwealth and the states and is now one of the largest items in the Budget.
explainer.why: Governments agreed the scheme's cost growth must slow to be sustainable. Missing the target means a larger share of taxes goes to one program, and less to everything else.

metrics.title: Business collapses
metrics.question: Are more businesses going under?

headline.caption: companies entering external administration for the first time

metrics.status_rule: Off track if company insolvencies are above the pre-COVID 2018–19 level.
context: Insolvencies rose from 4,912 in 2021–22 to 7,942, then 11,053, then 14,722 in 2024–25, 82% above the pre-COVID level.
2020–21 and 2021–22 were unusually low because of temporary COVID insolvency relief, so we compare with 2018–19.
ASIC recorded 12,819 in the first 11 months of 2025–26 (to 31 May 2026).

sources.title: Insolvency statistics Series 1 (published 8 September 2022)
Corporate Insolvency Update, Issue 37
Corporate Insolvency Update, Issue 40 (June 2026)

metrics.method: ASIC Series 1: companies entering external administration or having a controller appointed for the first time, by financial year.

explainer.what: The number of companies entering formal insolvency (administration, liquidation or receivership) for the first time each year, as recorded by the corporate regulator ASIC.
explainer.why: Business failures mean lost jobs, unpaid suppliers and owners losing their livelihoods. A sustained rise is a warning sign about costs, tax debts and the health of small business.

metrics.title: Power bills: the $275 promise
metrics.question: Did household power bills fall by $275 as promised?

headline.caption: a year: rise in the default power price for a typical NSW household (Ausgrid)

metrics.status_rule: Off track if the regulated default electricity offer in each benchmark region is higher, not $275 lower, than when the promise was made.
context: Default Market Offer, 2022–23 to 2026–27: NSW (Ausgrid) $1,512 → $1,899; South-East Queensland (Energex) $1,620 → $1,988; South Australia $1,840 → $2,334.
Victorian Default Offer: $1,403 → $1,591 over the same period.
The default offers are price caps on standing offers set by regulators for a typical household. Many households are on cheaper market offers, and the caps don't include government rebates.

promise.quote: It will cut power bills … by $275 a year for homes by 2025, compared to today.
promise.attribution: Labor's Powering Australia plan announcement, 3 December 2021. Source: RMIT ABC Fact Check and Labor media release.

chart.note: Change in annual default electricity offer, 2022–23 to 2026–27 ($ a year, incl. GST), compared with the promised $275 cut.

sources.title: Default Market Offer prices 2026–27: final determination
Default Market Offer price determination 2022–23: final determination
Victorian Default Offer 2026–27: final decision
Victorian Default Offer 2022–23: final decision
Promise check: cut power bills by $275

metrics.method: Annual bill at benchmark usage for residential customers on a flat tariff without controlled load (GST inclusive), from the regulators' final determinations. Change = 2026–27 minus 2022–23.

explainer.what: Each year energy regulators set a 'default offer', a maximum price for households on standard electricity contracts, based on typical usage in each region. It is the most consistent official yardstick for what a typical power bill costs.
explainer.why: Before the 2022 election, Labor promised its energy plan would cut household power bills by $275 a year by 2025. The regulators' own numbers show whether that happened.

metrics.title: Wholesale gas prices
metrics.question: Have east-coast wholesale gas prices come down from the 2022 crisis?
metrics.status_rule: On track if the average east-coast wholesale gas price is below its June quarter 2022 level.
context: Wholesale gas prices hit a record $28.40/GJ in the June quarter 2022 during the global energy crisis after Russia invaded Ukraine. They have since fallen to $9.08/GJ, the lowest since mid-2021.
A temporary $12/GJ emergency price cap was introduced from 23 December 2022.
The ACCC says long-term contract prices are around $13–15/GJ, which is what many businesses pay. Lower wholesale gas has not flowed through to lower electricity bills (see the $275 promise).

chart.note: Selected quarters reported by AEMO Quarterly Energy Dynamics.

sources.title: Quarterly Energy Dynamics Q2 2026
Quarterly Energy Dynamics Q2 2022
Storage vital to meeting winter demand across east coast gas market in Q3 2026

metrics.method: Average east-coast wholesale gas price for the quarter as reported in AEMO's Quarterly Energy Dynamics.

explainer.what: The average price of gas traded in east-coast wholesale markets, in dollars per gigajoule. It is a key input cost for manufacturers, gas-fired power stations and household gas bills.
explainer.why: We report the good news too. Wholesale gas has fallen sharply from its 2022 peak, but households haven't seen that in their electricity bills.

metrics.title: Emissions target
metrics.question: Is Australia on track for the government's legislated 43% emissions cut by 2030?
metrics.status_rule: Off track if the government's own latest projections show the 2030 target will not be met.
context: Emissions were 455.6 million tonnes CO2-e in the year to March 2026, 25.0% below 2005 levels.
The government's 2025 Annual Climate Change Statement projects a 42% reduction by 2030, short of the 43% target it legislated.

chart.note: Reduction below 2005 emissions levels. A land-sector recalculation in 2026 lowered reported reductions, so don't compare this with figures published earlier.

sources.title: Quarterly Update of Australia's National Greenhouse Gas Inventory: March 2026

sources.publisher: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
sources.title: Annual Climate Change Statement 2025

metrics.method: National inventory emissions (year to March 2026) compared with 2005, and the government's published 2030 projection.

explainer.what: Australia's total greenhouse gas emissions compared with 2005 levels, from the official national inventory. The Climate Change Act 2022 sets a target of a 43% reduction by 2030.
explainer.why: It is the government's own legislated target, and it has justified energy policy and spending decisions by it. Missing it on its own projections is a test of delivery.

metrics.title: Defence spending
metrics.question: Is Australia spending enough on defence in a more dangerous region?

headline.caption: of GDP on defence (traditional budget measure)

benchmark.label: Level the US has asked Australia to reach

metrics.status_rule: Off track if defence funding is below 3.5% of GDP, the level the US Defense Secretary asked Australia to reach 'as soon as possible' in 2025 and the core defence benchmark NATO allies adopted in 2025.
context: On the traditional budget measure, defence funding was 1.98% of GDP in 2021–22, 2.03% in 2024–25, and is 2.02% in 2026–27 ($62.6 billion).
In April 2026 the government said defence spending would reach 3% of GDP by 2033 'under the NATO approach', which counts more items than the traditional measure.
In June 2025 the Pentagon said Australia should increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP 'as soon as possible'.

chart.note: Budget-time figures as reported by defence analysts (2025–26 estimated actual; 2026–27 budget). Traditional appropriation measure.

Funding NATO (defence spending benchmarks)

metrics.method: Defence funding as a share of GDP on the traditional budget appropriation measure, as calculated and reported by defence budget analysts at each Budget. Defence's own budget statements publish dollars only.

explainer.what: How much the Commonwealth spends on the Australian Defence Force and the Department of Defence, as a share of the economy. Figures vary by method: the 'NATO approach' counts extra items such as some veterans' and security spending.
explainer.why: Allies and defence analysts have warned that Australia's strategic environment is the most dangerous in decades. Spending as a share of GDP is the standard way to compare commitment over time and across countries.

metrics.title: Laws passed
metrics.question: How much legislation has Parliament passed under this government?

headline.caption: Acts of Parliament passed in the government's first term

metrics.status_rule: Context only: the number of laws passed is not in itself good or bad, so this measure is not rated.
context: The 47th Parliament passed 354 Acts, against 407 in the 46th Parliament and 402 in the 45th.
Since the 48th Parliament opened on 22 July 2025, 133 Acts have received assent (to 11 September 2026).

chart.note: Acts assented, counted from the Federal Register of Legislation by assent date.

sources.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation (Office of Parliamentary Counsel)
sources.title: Acts collection: search by year of assent
47th Parliament statistics

metrics.method: Count of Acts in the Federal Register of Legislation by assent date within each Parliament's term. Cross-checked against the Parliamentary Education Office's 47th Parliament statistics (355 bills passed both houses).

explainer.what: The number of Acts, laws passed by both houses of Parliament and given Royal Assent, in each term of Parliament.
explainer.why: More laws aren't automatically better. This gives context on how busy the legislative agenda has been. Each new law typically needs public servants to administer it and imposes compliance obligations on the community.

metrics.title: GP bulk billing
metrics.question: Can Australians see a GP without paying?
metrics.status_rule: Watch if the GP bulk billing rate is below the government's promised 90%.
context: The annual GP bulk billing rate fell from 88.3% in 2021–22 to 77.3% in 2023–24, then recovered to 80.9% in 2025–26. The 2021–22 rate was inflated by COVID-era mandatory bulk billing for some patients.
The average out-of-pocket cost for a GP visit that isn't bulk billed rose from $42.25 in 2021–22 to $55.25 in 2025–26.
The quarterly rate has recovered from a low of 75.6% in October 2023 to 84.1% in the June quarter 2026.

sources.publisher: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
sources.title: Medicare annual statistics: state and territory, 2009–10 to 2025–26
Strengthening Medicare: bulk billing on the up
Delivering bulk billing for all Australians

metrics.method: Share of non-referred GP attendances that were bulk billed, by financial year (Medicare statistics). Latest quarterly rate from the Health Minister's release.

explainer.what: The share of GP visits where the doctor bills Medicare directly, so the patient pays nothing out of pocket.
explainer.why: Cost is a barrier to seeing a doctor. When bulk billing falls, people delay care and end up in emergency departments. The government has promised 9 in 10 GP visits will be bulk billed by 2030.

migration.program_note: 2026–27 planning levels: Skill 132,240, Family 52,460 and Special Eligibility 300 (185,000 in total), plus a separate Humanitarian Program of 20,000. Per-person values are Treasury's central lifetime estimates (2018–19 dollars, federal and state budgets combined).

evidence.source: Parliamentary Budget Office, 2026–27 Medium-Term Budget Outlook (2026), section 2.3
evidence.finding: Net migration 40,000 a year higher than forecast would improve the federal budget by about $80.6 billion over the medium term to 2036–37; 40,000 lower would worsen it by about $79.1 billion. The gain comes mainly from income tax, partly offset by extra grants to the states for things like schools. The PBO notes state budgets face their own costs and gains from extra demand for health, education, housing and infrastructure.

evidence.source: Parliamentary Budget Office, Election Commitments Report ECR-2025-2038 (2025)
evidence.finding: Cutting the permanent program from 185,000 to 140,000 places (rising back to 160,000 by 2028–29) was costed at about $3.4 billion worse for the budget over four years and $23.6 billion to 2035–36, before interest. Lower income tax and visa charges outweigh savings on benefits and services.

evidence.source: Treasury, The lifetime fiscal impact of the Australian permanent migration program (2021)
evidence.finding: Over their lifetimes, the average permanent migrant is about $127,000 more positive for federal and state budgets than the average Australian. It varies a lot by stream: skilled migrants about +$198,000 each, family migrants about −$126,000, humanitarian entrants about −$400,000. Parent visas cost about $391,000–$394,000 each. Temporary visa holders are positive over their stay, from about $200 (students, not counting their fees) to about $38,600 (temporary skilled workers). The results are sensitive to assumptions, so Treasury stresses the comparison between groups more than the absolute figures.

evidence.source: Productivity Commission, Migrant Intake into Australia, Inquiry Report No. 77 (2016)
evidence.finding: Across countries, migration's net effect on government budgets is usually within 2% of GDP either way. Skilled migrants are roughly on par with the existing population, family and humanitarian migrants contribute less, and temporary migrants contribute positively. It estimated each parent visa holder's net lifetime cost at $335,000–$410,000, with the visa charge covering only a fraction.

evidence.source: Centre for Population, 2025 Population Statement, Box 1
evidence.finding: A one-year fall in net migration of about 100,000 would cut the population aged 15 and over by about 0.4% and, over time, leave the economy (GDP) about 0.4% smaller, assuming productivity and participation don't change.

With net migration 50,000 a year higher from 2031–32 (combined with higher fertility), the economy would be about 7¾% larger by 2062–63, but real GDP per person would be almost unchanged: $131,900 against $131,800 in the baseline, or $131,500 with lower migration. Gross debt would be lower (25.4% of GDP against 32.1%). No productivity effect is modelled.

evidence.source: Productivity Commission, Migrant Intake into Australia (2016)
evidence.finding: Its illustrative modelling found migration at the long-run average would leave GDP per person about 7% higher by 2060 than zero net migration, mainly because migrants are younger. It cautions that GDP per person is an incomplete measure of wellbeing, and that income kept by Australians can gain less than GDP.

evidence.source: Breunig, Deutscher and To, Economic Record 93(301), 2017
evidence.finding: Studying 2001–2013, the authors found almost no evidence that immigration harmed the wages or employment of people born in Australia, once education and experience are taken into account.

evidence.source: Brell and Dustmann, Reserve Bank of Australia Annual Conference (2019)
evidence.finding: Reviewing the Australian research, they describe the evidence as sparse but generally not showing harm to average wages or to the wages of low-skilled Australians.

evidence.source: Productivity Commission, Migrant Intake into Australia (2016)
evidence.finding: Found recent migration had a negligible effect on the wages, employment and participation of existing workers overall, while noting earlier findings that specific groups of workers could face higher unemployment or slower wage growth.

evidence.source: Review of the Migration System, Final Report (2023)
evidence.finding: Found clear evidence of systemic exploitation of temporary migrant workers and warned of an emerging 'permanently temporary' group. Temporary migrant numbers had doubled since 2007 to about 1.8 million.

evidence.source: Reserve Bank of Australia, Bulletin, International Students and the Australian Economy (July 2025)
evidence.finding: The RBA's housing models suggest a 50,000 increase in population would raise private rents by about 0.5%. Newcomers add to demand for housing and goods sooner than they add to supply, though the two effects largely offset over the medium term.

evidence.source: Saunders and Tulip, Reserve Bank Research Discussion Paper 2019-01
evidence.finding: The 2005–08 population surge (adult population growth rising from 1.5% to 2.4% a year) left real rents about 9% higher in 2018 than they would otherwise have been.

evidence.source: National Housing Supply and Affordability Council, State of the Housing System 2025
evidence.finding: About 177,000 homes were completed in 2024, short of underlying demand of about 223,000. The average household was 2.54 people in September 2024.

evidence.source: Productivity Commission, Migrant Intake into Australia (2016)
evidence.finding: Migration pushes up land and housing prices, which benefits existing owners but lowers living standards for people trying to enter the property market. It also adds to congestion in the major cities, and the Commission found governments had not planned infrastructure well.
Net overseas migration was 306,000 in 2024–25, down from 429,000 a year earlier. The median age of migrant arrivals was 26.

Migrants are younger than the population on average (76% of new migrants in 2021–22 were aged 15–34, against 27% of the existing population), so migration slows population ageing. Treasury notes it offsets but does not resolve ageing, because migrants age too.
